::: {.lead}
*Byte Bay* is making *Marble Peak*, a game for phones. The player tilts the
phone, and a marble rolls down a mountain path. Before the team writes any
code, it asks: what is inside a phone, and what can the game use? A phone
has one main chip that does almost all the work, small **sensors** that
feel how the player moves it, a screen that feels fingers, and a battery
that runs out. In Seminar 2 you read spec sheets; in lecture 3
you met input and output devices. In this lesson you look inside the phone
and describe each part and its job in a game. Every section ends with a
short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary soc chipset npu modem sensor accelerometer gyroscope gps capacitive-touch-screen touch-sampling-rate battery-capacity thermal-throttling >}}

## 4.1 Why a phone has one main chip: the SoC

In Seminar 2 you opened a PC: a CPU, a graphics card and memory sticks, each
on its own. Open a phone, and you find almost everything on one small chip.
A phone has no room for a graphics card, no fan, and only a small battery.
So the makers put the main parts together on one chip. It is smaller, it
uses less energy, and the parts are close together, so data moves fast.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 4.1 — System on a chip (SoC)"}
A **system on a chip (SoC)** is one chip that holds the main parts of a
computer: the CPU cores, the GPU, the modem and the memory controller. On a spec sheet it is the **Chipset** line.
:::

![The parts of an SoC. The RAM sits next to it and is shared by the CPU and the GPU.](images/soc-map.png){#fig-soc width=96%}

| Part of the SoC | Its job | In a game |
|---|---|---|
| CPU cores | run the program | the rules, the physics, the enemies |
| GPU | draws the pictures | every frame of the game |
| modem | mobile data (4G, 5G) | online matches, the leaderboard |
| image processor | camera pictures | AR and photo modes |
| memory controller | moves data to and from the RAM | textures from the RAM to the GPU |

: The parts of an SoC and their jobs (@fig-soc). {#tbl-soc}

The RAM is a separate chip next to the SoC (often on top of it). The CPU and
the GPU **share** it: a phone has no separate video memory (lecture 3). A
phone with 8 GB of RAM uses the same 8 GB for the game's code and for its
textures. Common SoC families are Qualcomm Snapdragon, MediaTek Dimensity
and Helio, Samsung Exynos, Google Tensor and Apple's A-series.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.1 — One frame of Marble Peak"}
1. The CPU cores read the tilt and move the marble (physics).
2. The GPU draws the mountain, the marble and the light.
3. Both use the same RAM: the code of the game and the textures are there.
4. At the end of a level, the modem sends the time to the online leaderboard.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Judging a phone by its number of cores. Two phones can both have "8 cores",
but one SoC has a much stronger GPU. For games, the GPU part of the SoC often
matters more than the number of CPU cores.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/soc-explorer.html" poster="sims/soc-explorer.png" title="SoC Explorer: the parts of a phone's main chip" height="640" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The SoC of your phone"}
Find the name of the SoC in your phone.

- **Android:** open **Settings → About phone**. Some phones show
  **Processor** or **Chipset**. If yours does not, search the model name on
  the maker's website and look for "chipset" or "processor".
- **iPhone:** open **Settings → General → About** and read the **Model
  Name**. Apple's website lists the chip of each model (for example "A15
  Bionic").

*Your result:* the model of your phone, the name of its SoC and the company
that made the SoC.

::: {.check}
A good answer names the model, the SoC and its maker, for example "Galaxy
A55, Exynos 1480, Samsung" or "iPhone 13, A15 Bionic, Apple". Check: the SoC
is the Chipset (or Chip) line of the maker's spec page.
:::
:::

## 4.2 How the phone feels the player: sensors

In *Marble Peak* the player does not touch the screen to steer: the player
tilts the phone. Which part of the phone feels the tilt? A phone is full of
small **sensors** (@fig-sensors).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 4.2 — Sensor"}
A **sensor** is a small part that measures something in the world, such as
movement, light or position, and turns it into numbers. Sensors are input
devices (lecture 3).
:::

![The main sensors of a phone and what games do with them.](images/sensors.png){#fig-sensors width=96%}

The two sensors that games use most measure different things:

- The **accelerometer** measures acceleration, and it always feels gravity.
  When the phone lies flat, gravity pulls straight "into" the screen: about
  9.8 m/s² on the z-axis and 0 on x and y. When you tilt the phone, part of
  gravity moves to x or y. So the accelerometer shows the **tilt** and a
  **shake**.
- The **gyroscope** measures how fast the phone **turns**, in degrees per
  second. When the phone stays still, it reads 0, even when the phone is
  tilted.

The **GPS** finds the position of the phone on Earth, and the **compass**
(magnetometer) finds north. The camera and the microphone are sensors too.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.2 — Which sensor for which game?"}
1. A racing game where you steer by tilting: the **accelerometer**.
2. A shooter where you aim by turning the phone: the **gyroscope**.
3. "Shake the phone to roll the dice": the **accelerometer**.
4. An AR pet that stays on your table while you walk around it: the
   **camera**, the **gyroscope** and the **accelerometer** together.
5. A treasure hunt on the streets of your city: the **GPS**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"The gyroscope measures the tilt." A tilted phone that lies still on a book
gives a gyroscope value of 0: it does not turn. The tilt comes from the
accelerometer. Also, not every phone has every sensor: many cheap phones
have no gyroscope. A game that needs one cannot run there (a compatibility
problem, Seminar 3), so it must offer another control.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/tilt-lab.html" poster="sims/tilt-lab.png" title="Tilt Lab: the accelerometer and the gyroscope" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your phone's sensors in Tilt Lab"}
Open **Tilt Lab** on your phone (scan its QR code) and press **Use the
sensors**. (If your phone gives no values, use the drag pad.)

1. Lay the phone flat on the table. Write x, y and z.
2. Tilt the phone to the left and hold it still. Write x and the gyroscope.
3. Turn the phone quickly. What does the gyroscope show now?

*Your result:* three readings, and one sentence on the difference between
the two sensors.

::: {.check}
When you tilt the phone, the accelerometer values change and stay changed
while you hold it tilted. When you turn the phone, the gyroscope values move
and go back to about 0 when it stops turning.
:::
:::

## 4.3 How the screen feels a finger

Two testers write to Byte Bay. One says: "With gloves, the game does not
react." The other says: "On my old phone, my taps feel a little late." Both
are about the touch screen.

Most phones have a **capacitive touch screen**: under the glass there is a
grid of very thin wires (@fig-touch). The finger carries a tiny electric
charge, so it changes the charge where it touches the grid. A small
controller finds this place and sends its position to the game. It finds
several fingers at once (multi-touch, lecture 3).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 4.3 — Touch sampling rate"}
The **touch sampling rate** is how many times per second the screen checks
for touches, in hertz (Hz). At 120 Hz it checks about every 8 ms; at
240 Hz about every 4 ms.
:::

![A grid of wires finds the finger. A screen that checks more often finds a tap sooner.](images/touch-grid.png){#fig-touch width=96%}

Do not mix up the touch sampling rate with the **refresh rate** (lecture 3):
the refresh rate is how often the *picture* changes; the touch sampling
rate is how often the screen *reads* the fingers. Many phones check touches
twice as often as they draw: 60 Hz picture with 120 Hz touch, or 120 Hz
picture with 240 Hz touch.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.3 — The two testers"}
1. Gloves: cloth does not carry the charge of the finger, so the grid feels
   nothing. Special touch gloves have conductive threads in the fingertips.
   A wet screen can also confuse the grid.
2. Late taps: the old phone checks touches at 120 Hz, the new one at 240 Hz.
   A tap can wait up to about 8 ms on the old phone and 4 ms on the new one.
   In a rhythm game, the player can feel such small delays.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that a 120 Hz screen reads touches 120 times per second. The
refresh rate (picture) and the touch sampling rate (fingers) are two
different numbers. The spec sheet lists them on two lines, if it gives the
touch sampling rate at all.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Test your touch screen"}
Open a drawing app or the notes app on your phone.

1. Draw with a fingertip, then with a fingernail, then with the back of a
   pencil, then through a paper tissue. Which ones work?
2. Look for the refresh rate setting. Android: **Settings → Display**, then
   **Motion smoothness** (Samsung) or **Smooth display** or **Refresh rate**
   (other phones). iPhone: there is no setting; Pro models change their
   refresh rate up to 120 Hz by themselves.

*Your result:* a table of four objects (works or not) and the refresh rate
of your phone.

::: {.check}
Only the fingertip works: the screen feels the electric charge of the skin,
and a nail, a pencil or a tissue does not carry it. Many Android phones offer
60 Hz and 90 or 120 Hz (Smooth display); an iPhone has no setting.
:::
:::

## 4.4 How long can the player play? Battery and heat

A tester plays *Marble Peak* on a bus. After 20 minutes, the frame rate
falls from 60 to 45 fps, and the phone feels hot. After about 5 hours, the
battery is empty. Why?

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 4.4 — Battery capacity"}
The **battery capacity** is the amount of charge in the battery, in
milliampere-hours (mAh). A game draws a **current**, in milliamperes (mA).
The play time is about
$$\text{play time (hours)} = \text{capacity (mAh)} \div \text{current (mA)}.$$
:::

![5000 mAh at 1000 mA last about 5 hours. When the SoC gets hot, it slows down.](images/battery.png){#fig-battery width=96%}

Three things use most of the power in a game (@fig-battery): the **screen**
(more for high brightness and a high refresh rate), the **SoC** (more for a
high frame rate and high graphics), and the **radios** (mobile data, GPS).
The SoC also turns this power into heat. A phone has no fan, so when it gets
too hot, the SoC slows itself down to protect itself: **thermal throttling**
(lecture 3). The frame rate drops.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.4 — Play time"}
1. The test phone has 5000 mAh. *Marble Peak* draws 1000 mA:
   5000 ÷ 1000 = **5 hours**.
2. With the screen at low brightness, the game draws only 500 mA:
   5000 ÷ 500 = **10 hours**.
3. A phone with 4000 mAh, at the same 500 mA: 4000 ÷ 500 = **8 hours**.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.5 — Hot after 20 minutes"}
1. At 60 fps the SoC works hard. After 20 minutes it is hot.
2. It slows down (thermal throttling), and the game falls to 45 fps.
3. Byte Bay adds a setting "30 fps (battery saver)": less work for the SoC,
   less heat, longer play.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"A bigger mAh number makes the phone faster." The capacity only says how
much charge the battery holds. It says nothing about the speed of the SoC.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/battery-lab.html" poster="sims/battery-lab.png" title="Battery Lab: play time and heat" height="600" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Battery use on your phone"}
1. On your phone, open the battery page. Android: **Settings → Battery →
   Battery usage**. iPhone: **Settings → Battery**. Which three apps used
   the most battery today?
2. In **Battery Lab**, find settings that give at least 6 hours with 5000
   mAh and keep the phone cool.

*Your result:* the three apps with their percentages, and your settings in
Battery Lab with their play time.

::: {.check}
A good answer names three apps from the battery list (games and video apps
are often at the top). In Battery Lab, 6 hours or more need less power, for
example 30 fps, a darker screen and Wi-Fi instead of mobile data; the phone
stays cool with fewer frames.
:::
:::

## Case study: Marble Peak

*Byte Bay* tests *Marble Peak* on its test phone T1. The spec sheet of T1
says: chipset with 8 CPU cores (up to 3.0 GHz) and a GPU; 8 GB of
RAM; a 120 Hz screen with a touch sampling rate of 240 Hz; a 5000 mAh
battery; sensors: accelerometer, gyroscope, compass and GPS. The game reads
the **accelerometer** to roll the marble. At 60 fps with a bright screen, it
draws 1000 mA, so the battery lasts about 5 hours. After 20 minutes the SoC
is hot, and the game falls to 45 fps. The Game challenge of the interactive
lesson uses these facts. In the mini-game below you roll the marble yourself:
with your phone's accelerometer, or with the pad.

{{< sim file="sims/marble-peak.html" poster="sims/marble-peak.png" title="Marble Peak: tilt to roll the marble" kind="game" height="720" >}}

## Further reading

Tanenbaum and Austin, *Structured Computer Organization*, 6th ed., Chapter 1
(the computer zoo: embedded and mobile computers) and Chapter 3 on chips.
The Android Developers documentation, "Sensors overview"; Apple Developer
documentation, "Core Motion".

## Exercises

1. What is an SoC? Name four of its parts.
2. Which part of the SoC draws the frames of a game? Which part sends the
   score to an online leaderboard?
3. Why does a phone have no separate video memory?
4. Which sensor does each game use: (a) steer by tilting; (b) aim by turning
   the phone; (c) a treasure hunt in the city?
5. A tilted phone lies still on a book. What does the gyroscope show? Why?
6. Why does a touch screen not react to a finger in a normal glove?
7. A phone has a 60 Hz screen and a touch sampling rate of 120 Hz. What does
   each number mean?
8. A phone has 4500 mAh. A game draws 900 mA. About how long can the player
   play?
9. Why does the frame rate of a game fall after 20 minutes on some phones?
   What can the game do?
10. *Marble Peak*: which sensor rolls the marble, and how long does the
    battery of T1 last at 1000 mA?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. One chip with the main parts of a computer; for example CPU cores, GPU, modem, image processor and memory controller.
2. The GPU; the modem.
3. The CPU and the GPU are on the same chip and share the RAM next to it.
4. (a) the accelerometer; (b) the gyroscope; (c) the GPS.
5. 0: the gyroscope measures turning, and the phone does not turn. The tilt shows in the accelerometer.
6. The cloth does not carry the charge of the finger, so the grid under the glass feels nothing.
7. The picture changes 60 times per second; the screen checks for touches 120 times per second.
8. 4500 ÷ 900 = 5 hours.
9. The SoC gets hot and slows down (thermal throttling). The game can offer a lower frame rate (30 fps) or lower graphics.
10. The accelerometer; 5000 ÷ 1000 = 5 hours.
:::
